entries.0244ce467445838e130d95b506928eadca8772bf: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.10.27" sID="gen118935" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> <hi type="italic">If any one of them that believe not invites you.</hi> Here follows an exception, to this effect, that if a believer has been warned, that what is set before him has been offered to an idol, and sees that there is a danger of offense being given, he sins against the brethren if he does not abstain. He shows then, in short, that care must be taken not to hurt weak consciences.<div eID="gen118936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118937" type="x-p"/>When he says — <hi type="italic">and you are willing to go</hi>, he intimates indirectly, that he does not altogether approve of it, and that it would be better if they declined, but as it is a thing indifferent, he does not choose to forbid it absolutely. And, certainly, there could be nothing better than to keep at a distance from such snares — not that those are expressly to be condemned, who accommodate themselves to men only in so far as conscience permits, <note n="601"> <div sID="gen118938" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Seulement autant que faire se pent sans offenser Dieu</foreign>;” — “Only so far as they can do so without offending God.”<div eID="gen118938" type="x-p"/> </note> but because it becomes us to proceed with caution, <note n="602"> <div sID="gen118939" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Auec grand auis et prudence</foreign>;” — “With great care and prudence.”<div eID="gen118939" type="x-p"/> </note> where we see that we are in danger of falling.<div eID="gen118937" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118935" osisID="1Cor.10.27" type="section"/>
entries.e9cafcc7e1a5c2b95795e5446fb1f754fb97220e: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.10.29" sID="gen118940" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> <hi type="italic">Conscience, I say, not thine own</hi> He always carefully takes heed not to diminish liberty, or to appear to take from it in any degree. “Thou oughtest to bear with the weak conscience of thy brother, that thou mayest not abuse thy right, so as to give occasion of offense to him; but in the meantime thy conscience remains, nevertheless, free, because it is exempted from that subjection. Let not, therefore, the restraint which I impose upon thee as to outward use, become by any means a snare to entangle thy conscience.”<div eID="gen118941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118942" type="x-p"/>It must be observed here, that the term <hi type="italic">conscience</hi> is taken here in its strict acceptation; for in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.13.5">Romans 13:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.5">1 Timothy 1:5</reference>, it is taken in a larger sense. “We ought, says Paul, to obey princes, <hi type="italic">not merely for the sake of wrath</hi>,<hi type="italic"> but also for that of conscience</hi>” — that is, not merely from fear of punishment, but because the Lord orders it so, and it is our duty. Is it not reasonable, too, that we should for the same reason accommodate ourselves to weak brethren — that is, because we are to this extent subject to them in the sight of God? Farther, <hi type="italic">the end of the commandment is love out of a good conscience</hi> Is not the affection of <hi type="italic">love</hi> included in a <hi type="italic">good conscience?</hi> Hence its meaning here is, as I have already stated, more restricted, inasmuch as the soul of a pious man looks exclusively to the tribunal of God, has no regard to men, is satisfied with the blessing of liberty procured for it by Christ, and is bound to no individuals, and to no circumstances of time or place.<div eID="gen118942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118943" type="x-p"/>Some manuscripts repeat the statement — <hi type="italic">The earth is the Lord’s.</hi> But the probability is, that some reader having put it on the margin, it had crept into the text. <note n="603"> <div sID="gen118944" type="x-p"/> It is omitted in the Alex., Clermont, and in all of the more ancient MSS.; and in the Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate versions. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen118944" type="x-p"/> </note> It is not, however, a matter of great importance.<div eID="gen118943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118945" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For why is my liberty</hi> It is doubtful, whether Paul speaks in this way of himself, or whether he makes this objection in the name of the Corinthians. If we take it as spoken in his own name, it will be a confirmation of the preceding statement. “In restricting yourself, for the sake of another man’s conscience, your liberty is not thereby made subject to him.” If in the name of the Corinthians, the meaning will be this: “You impose upon us an unjust law, in requiring that our liberty should stand or fall at the caprice of others.” I am of opinion, that Paul says this of himself, but explains it in another way, for hitherto I have been stating the views of others. To be <hi type="italic">judged</hi>, then, I explain here as meaning — to be <hi type="italic">condemned</hi>, agreeably to the common acceptation of the word in Scripture. Paul warns us of the danger that must ensue, if we make use of our liberty unreservedly, so as to give occasion of offense to our neighbors — that they will <hi type="italic">condemn </hi>it. Thus, through our fault, and our unreasonableness, the consequence will be, that this special benefit from God will be <hi type="italic">condemned</hi> If we do not guard against this danger, we corrupt our liberty by our abuse of it. This consideration, then, tends very much to confirm Paul’s exhortation.<div eID="gen118945" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118940" osisID="1Cor.10.29" type="section"/>
entries.f3c5f1ac372baf1472b0b268d331cc1052de0910: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.10.30" sID="gen118946" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">If therefore by grace.</hi> This argument is similar to the preceding one, or nearly so. “As it is owing to the kindness of God that <hi type="italic">all things are lawful for me,</hi> why should I act in such a manner, that it should be reckoned to my account as a vice?” We cannot, it is true, prevent the wicked from reviling us, nor even the weak from being sometimes displeased with us; but Paul here reproves the forwardness of those, who of their own accord give occasion of offense, and hurt weak consciences, when neither necessity or expediency calls for it. He would have us, then, make a good use of our benefits, <note n="604"> <div sID="gen118948" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est a dire, de nestre liberte</foreign>;” — “That is to say, of our liberty.”<div eID="gen118948" type="x-p"/> </note> that the weak may not have occasion of reviling from our inconsiderate use of liberty.<div eID="gen118947" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118946" osisID="1Cor.10.30" type="section"/>
entries.35a25666fb00def1b45ea38cbef040f85ae5719f: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.10.31" sID="gen118949" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31.</hi> <hi type="italic">Whether, therefore, ye eat, or drink</hi> Lest they should think, that in so small a matter they should not be so careful to avoid blame, he teaches that there is no part of our life, and no action so minute, <note n="605"> <div sID="gen118951" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qu’il n’y a rien en toute nostre vie, tant petit soit-il</foreign>;” — “That there is nothing in our whole life, be it ever so small.”<div eID="gen118951" type="x-p"/> </note> that it ought not to be directed to the glory of God, and that we must take care that, even in eating and drinking, we may aim at the advancement of it. This statement is connected with what goes before; for if we are eagerly desirous of the glory of God, as it becomes us to be, we will never allow, so far as we can prevent it, his benefits to lie under reproach. It was well expressed anciently in a common proverb, that we must not <hi type="italic">live to eat</hi>; but <hi type="italic">eat to live</hi> <note n="606"> <div sID="gen118952" type="x-p"/> The proverbial expression referred to occurs in Auctor. ad Herenn. 4. 28: — “<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Esse </hi>oportet ut <hi type="italic">vivas</hi>, non <hi type="italic">vivere </hi>ut <hi type="italic">edas</hi></foreign>;” — “You should <hi type="italic">eat to live</hi> — not<hi type="italic"> live </hi>to <hi type="italic">eat</hi>.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen118952" type="x-p"/> </note> Provided the end of living be at the same time kept in view, the consequence will thus be, that our food will be in a manner sacred to God, inasmuch as it will be set apart for his service.<div eID="gen118950" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118949" osisID="1Cor.10.31" type="section"/>
entries.6d38e5a44837f979a4f51c10b54c30373105c4e0: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.10.32" sID="gen118953" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32.</hi> <hi type="italic">Be not occasions of stumbling to any</hi> This is the <hi type="italic">second </hi>point, which it becomes us to have an eye to — the rule of love. A desire, then, for the glory of God, holds the <hi type="italic">first </hi>place; a regard to our neighbor holds the <hi type="italic">second</hi> He makes mention of <hi type="italic">Jews and Gentiles</hi>, not merely because the Church of God consisted of those two classes, but to teach us that we are debtors to all, even to strangers, that we may, if possible, <hi type="italic">gain </hi>them. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.9.20 Bible:1Cor.9.21">1 Corinthians 9:20, 21</reference>.)<div eID="gen118954" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.10.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118953" osisID="1Cor.10.32" type="section"/>
entries.134764f4aa613e8a0bff85a4864c9401077628f9:
33. Even as I please all men in all this As he speaks in a general way, and without exception, some extend it by mistake to things that are unlawful, and at variance with the word of the Lord — as if it were allowable, for the sake of our neighbor, to venture farther than the Lord permits us. It is, however, more than certain, that Paul accommodated himself to men only in things indifferent, and in things lawful in themselves. Farther, the end must be carefully observed — that they may be saved Hence what is opposed to their salvation ought not to be conceded to them,
“I1 ne leur faut pas accorder, et s’accommoder a eux en cela;” — “It is not proper to concede to them, and to accommodate ourselves to them in that.”
but we must use prudence, and that of a spiritual kind.
The view here given by Calvin of the spirit by which Paul was actuated in this part of his conduct, is most successfully brought out, at greater length, by the Reverend Andrew Fuller, when comparing 1 Corinthians 10:33, with Galatians 1:10. — “Though both these kinds of action are expressed by one term — to please — yet they are exceedingly diverse; no less so than a conduct which has the glory of God and the good of mankind for its object, and one that originates and terminates in self. The former of these passages should be read in connection with what precedes and follows it, (1 Corinthians 10:31-33.) Hence it appears plain, that the things in which the Apostle pleased all, men, require to be restricted to such things as tend to their ‘profit, that they may be saved.’ Whereas the things in which, according to the latter passage, he could not please men, and yet be the servant of Christ, were of a contrary tendency. Such were the objects pursued by the false teachers whom he opposed, and who desired to ‘make a fair show in the flesh, lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.’ (1 Corinthians 6:12.) The former is that sweet inoffensiveness of spirit which teaches us to lay aside all selfwill and self-importance, that charity which ‘seeketh not her own,’ and ‘is not easily provoked;’ it is that spirit, in short, which the same writer elsewhere recommends from the example of Christ himself: ‘We, then, who are strong, ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let every one of us please his neighbor, for his good to edification: for even Christ pleased not himself; but, as it is written, The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me.’ But the latter spirit referred to is that sordid compliance with the corruptions of human nature, of which flatterers and deceivers have always availed themselves, not for the glory of God or the good of men, but for the promotion of their own selfish designs.” — Fullers Works, volume 3. — Ed.
CHAPTER 11
1 Corinthians 11:1-16
1. Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
1. Imitatores mei estote, sicut et ego Christi.
2. Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you.
2. Laudo autem vos, fratres, quod omnia mea meministis et traditiones
“Mes ordonnances;” — “My ordinances.”
tenetis, quemadmodum vobis tradidi.
3. But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.
3. Volo autem vos scire, quod omnis viri caput est Christus, caput autem mulieris, vir: caput autem Christi, Deus.
4. Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonoureth his head.
4. Omnis vir orans aut prophetans velato capite, dedecore afficit caput suum.
5. But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven.
5. Omnis mulier orans aut prophetans aperto capite, dedecore afticit caput suum: perinde enim acsi radatur.
6. For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered.
6. Si enim non velatur mulier, etiam tondeatur: si autem mulieri turpe est tonderi aut radi, veletur.
7. For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man.
7. Vir quidem velato esse capite non debet, quum sit imago et gloria Dei: mulier autem gloria viri est.
8. For the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man.
8. Non enim est virex muliere, sed mulier ex viro.
9. Neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man.
9. Etenim non est creatus vir mulieris causa, sed mulier causa viri.
10. For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.
10. Propterea debet mulier potestatem habere super caput suum, propter angelos.
11. Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord.
11. Caeterum neque vir absque muliere, neque mulier absque viro in Domino.
12. For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God.
12. Quemadmodum enim mulier ex viro, sic et vir per mulierem: olnnia autem ex Deo.
13. Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered?
13. In vobis ipsis iudicate, deceatne mulierem retecto capite Deum precari.
14. Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?
14. An ne ipsa quidem natura vos docet, quod si vir comam alat, dedecus illi sit?
15. But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering.
15. Si vero mulier comam alat, gloria sit illi? quoniam illi coma instar velamenti data est.
16. But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God.
16. Quodsi quis videtur contentiosus esse, nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, neque Ecclesiae Dei.

               <ns0:head>CHAP. X.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:447" />1 MOreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers were <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 9.18. Deut. 1.33. Neh. 9.12, 19. Psal. 78.14.</ns0:note> under the cloud <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle saw that many in this Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> were puffed up with their knowledge, and other gifts and great pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viledges with which God had blessed them; as also with the o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pinion of their being a Gospel-Church, and some of the first-fruits of the Gentiles unto Christ, and might therefore think, that they needed not to be pressed to such degrees of strictness and watchfulness; to beat them therefore off from this confi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence and vain presumption, the Apostle here sets before them the example of the Church of the Jews, when he tells them, <ns0:hi>he would not have them ignorant,</ns0:hi> his meaning is, he would have them know and remember, he would have them well acquaint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with, and to reflect upon this, That all the Jews in <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his time, whom he calls <ns0:hi>their Father's,</ns0:hi> not according to the flesh; for the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> were not descended from Jews, but with respect to the Covenant, and their relation they stood unto God, as they were the only people God had on Earth; these, he saith, were <ns0:hi>all of them</ns0:hi> (the whole Camp of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi>) under ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry great priviledges, of which he reckoneth divers, they were under the conduct of the Cloud, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 13.21.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 14.22. Josh. 4.23.</ns0:note> all passed through the sea <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">and they all obtained the favour of God so far for them, as to divide the Red sea, so as they passed through it upon dry ground.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud, and in the sea <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">There are two great difficulties in this verse: 1. <ns0:hi>What is meant by Moses.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>How and why the Israelites are said to be ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptized unto Moses.</ns0:hi> Some understand by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> the person of <ns0:hi>Moses:</ns0:hi> others, the Law or Doctrine of <ns0:hi>Moses.</ns0:hi> Those who by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> understand the person of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> are divided in their opi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nions, Whether the Preposition <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which signifieth divers things, were better translated <ns0:hi>by,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>into,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>unto,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>together with.</ns0:hi> Some think it were better translated <ns0:hi>by,</ns0:hi> and thus all the Jews were baptized by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> in the Cloud and in the Sea, that is, by his Ministry, and thus this very Particle is translated, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 7.53. & 19.3. Some think it were better translated <ns0:hi>in Moses,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> going before them, when they were under the conduct of the Cloud, and when they passed through the Red sea. Others judge it better translated <ns0:hi>into Moses,</ns0:hi> that is, either <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> going before them: or, 2. as <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> was a Type of Christ, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.19. Some would have the Particle here to sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifie <ns0:hi>together with.</ns0:hi> Others even unto <ns0:hi>Moses, Moses</ns0:hi> himself not being excepted from that Baptism in the Cloud and in the Sea. Others by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> here understand the Doctrine and Law of <ns0:hi>Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses:</ns0:hi> thus the term <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> is used, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 16.29. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 15.21. So they say, that to be baptized into <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> is to believe <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> so far, as to follow his conduct through the Sea, and under the Cloud. 2. The second difficulty, is to resolve what is meant by being <ns0:hi>baptized:</ns0:hi> the word signifieth in the common accepti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of it, a <ns0:hi>being washed</ns0:hi>; in the Ecclesiastical acception, it signifies an holy Institution of the New Testament, according to which Christians are initiated into the Church of God, by washing them <ns0:hi>In the Name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.</ns0:hi> Now how could the Jews be sad either to be washed (that is, ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptized) either in <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> or by <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> or with <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> or into <ns0:hi>Moses?</ns0:hi> Whenas the History of the Old Testament tells us, That both <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and all the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> went through the Sea on dry ground, and we do not read, that the Cloud under the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duct of which the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> journied, ever poured down any water with which the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> their Leader, could be washed. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Some think, that the Cloud which passing over the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> was all darkness to their Enemies, yet pour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed down water for the refreshing of the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> as it passed over their heads, and that this is hinted to us by the Psalmist, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68.7, 8, 9. Others think, that the Apostle applieth the term of <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> to a priviledge of which the old <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> had as much reason to glory, as the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> had of their Baptism, properly so called. Others say, that the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> walking un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the Cloud and through the Sea, which was darkness and destruction to their Adversaries, was a figure of Baptism, the Seal of the New Testament, by which Christs Victory over our spiritual Enemies is confirmed to us, and in that respect the Apostle maketh use of this term <ns0:hi>baptized.</ns0:hi> Others most proba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly think, that the Apostle useth this term, in regard of the great Analogy betwixt <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> (as it was then used) the per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons going down into the waters, and being dipped in them; and the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> going down into the Sea, the great receptacle of water, though the water at that time were gathered on heaps on either side of them; yet they seemed buried in the waters, as persons in that Age were when they were baptized, and for being baptized in the Cloud, there is a great probability that the Cloud did showre down rain, according to what is quoted out of the Psalmist.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And did all eat the same <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 16.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> spiritual meat <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Those of the Jews that perished in the Wilderness, did all eat the same <ns0:hi>Manna</ns0:hi> which <ns0:hi>Caleb</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ioshua</ns0:hi> a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e of, who went into <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi> Or those <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> that so perished in the Wilderness did eat the same <ns0:hi>spiritual meat</ns0:hi> that we do, they in the <ns0:hi>Type,</ns0:hi> we in the <ns0:hi>Antitype. Manna</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>spiritual meat:</ns0:hi> 1. Because it was bread came down from Heaven, the habitation of spiritual Beings, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6.31. 2. It was miraculously produced. 3. Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause it was Angels food given out by their ministry. 4. But principally, because it signified Christ, who was the true Bread from Heaven, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6.32.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And did all drink the same <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 7<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> spiritual drink <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">And all the Jews, as well those that perished in the Wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness, as those that were preserved to go into <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> they drank of the water which came out of the <ns0:hi>Rock,</ns0:hi> of which we read, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 17.6. <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 20.11. which water was <ns0:hi>spiritual drink</ns0:hi> in the same respects that the <ns0:hi>Manna</ns0:hi> was spiritual meat, being miraculously produced, and being a figure of Christ. For,</ns0:note>: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowed them, and that Rock-was Christ <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">saith the Apostle, <ns0:hi>That Rock was Christ,</ns0:hi> that is, that Rock did signifie or prefigure Christ, the Rock was Christ in the same sense that the <ns0:hi>Bread in the Lords Supper</ns0:hi> is the <ns0:hi>Body of Christ,</ns0:hi> that is, a sign which by Divine Institution did signifie Christ. Here ariseth a question in what sense it is said, <ns0:hi>That the Rock followed them?</ns0:hi> That by the Rock is to be understood the water that God made to flow out of the Rock, is evident; but though we read of water twice fetched out of the Rock upon <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> smiting of it, once at <ns0:hi>Rephidim,</ns0:hi> before they came so far as Mount <ns0:hi>Sinai, Exod.</ns0:hi> 17.6. another time at <ns0:hi>Cadesh, Num.</ns0:hi> 20.7, 8. yet we no where read in the History of the Jewish jour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neyings to <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> that the Rock followed them. But this is not the only thing that we read in the New Testament relating to the History of the Old Testament, with some circumstances which we do not find recorded there, it is enough that it is plainly asserted here, and it must be presumed, or how can we imagine, that the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were supplied with water for forty years together? Whereas some object, That if the water, which came out of the Rock at <ns0:hi>Rephidim,</ns0:hi> had followed them, there would have been no need of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> striking the Rock at <ns0:hi>Kadesh:</ns0:hi> It is answered, That God, to try them, probably caused the water to stop. For the Analogy betwixt the <ns0:hi>Rock</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Christ,</ns0:hi> Divines make it to lie in these particulars. 1. That <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> is the <ns0:hi>firm</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>unmoveable Foundation of his Church,</ns0:hi> called there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore a <ns0:hi>Stone,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>tried Stone, Isa.</ns0:hi> 28.16. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.33. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.6. 2. As this Rock sent out no water for the refreshment of the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> till <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> had struck it: So all the benefit we have from Christ as Mediator, floweth from him as <ns0:hi>smitten of God,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>afflicted.</ns0:hi> 3. As the water of the Rock served both for <ns0:hi>cleansing,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>upholding life</ns0:hi> in satisfying thirst: So the Blood of Christ is useful to the Soul, both for washing from the guilt of sin, and the upholding spiritual life in a Soul. 4. As the Rock that followed the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> afforded water not only to that ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neration that were alive and present when the Rock was smit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten, but to all the succeeding generations, until the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> came in <ns0:hi>Canaan:</ns0:hi> So the Blood of Christ is not useful only to his people in this or that place or Age, but to all that shall be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve in him, and that till they shall come into the heavenly <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:447" />5 But with many of them God was not well pleased <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">These <ns0:hi>many</ns0:hi> were no less than that whole generation, which were at that time twenty years old and upward, according to the threatning, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 14.28, 29. of the accomplishment of which we read, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 26.64, 65.</ns0:note>: for they were overthrown in the wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">as an instance of Gods being displeased with them, he giveth their falling in the Wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness It is very possible, that many of these were the ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jects of Gods eternal and special love, and eternally saved, not<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />withstanding their joyning with worser men, in their rebellion and murmuring; but that signal judgment of God upon them, was enough to prove, that their being baptized into <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> in the Cloud, and in the Sea, and being made partakers of those great priviledges of eating spiritual meat, and drinking spiritual drink, typifying Christ, did not set them out of the danger of Gods judgments, which is the use the Apostle maketh of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="7">7 Neither be ye idolaters, as <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> some of them <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The people of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> being first inticed to whoredom with the daughters of <ns0:hi>Moab,</ns0:hi> were after that, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 25.2. invited <ns0:hi>to the Sacrifices of their Gods, and did eat, and bowed down to their Gods.</ns0:hi> So, either worshipped the Creature instead of the Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tor, or worshipped the Creator in and by the Creature.</ns0:note>; as it is written, * The people sate down to eat and drink, and rose up to play <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Thus it is written in <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 32.6. (which History mentioneth another Idolatry) they were guilty of in worshipping the golden Calf.) They were wont to have Feasts after their Sacrifices, and pass<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times and diversions after such Feasts; and particularly we are told in the History concerning the golden Calf, that they <ns0:hi>danced</ns0:hi> before it. <ns0:hi>Stephen,</ns0:hi> Acts 7.41. saith, <ns0:hi>They rejoiced in the work <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>

               <ns0:p n="8">8 Neither let us commit fornication, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 29.</ns0:note> as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The story to which this verse relates is, that, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 25.1, 9. when <ns0:hi>Balaam</ns0:hi> could not curse the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> he advi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed the debauching of them by the <ns0:hi>Moabitish</ns0:hi> women, first in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticing them to Fornication and Adultery, then to Idolatry: and they were inticed, which caused a plague amongst them, which destroyed amongst them in <ns0:hi>one day three and twenty thou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sand</ns0:hi> (saith our Apostle,) <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> saith, that there dyed <ns0:hi>four and twenty thousand</ns0:hi>; there are many guesses for the clearing of that seeming contradiction: Some say, that <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> mentioneth not <ns0:hi>one day,</ns0:hi> there might in all dye 24000, but not all the <ns0:hi>same day,</ns0:hi> nor possibly by the same death. But nothing is in Scripture more ordinary, than to speak of things or persons in round numbers, though something over or under; and also to speak according to the common reckoning of people, who also may tal<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> variously. Some might report 23, some 24000: or possi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> chose to mention the lesser, rather than the greater round number. The sense of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> might be about 24000, or near up to that number, all of which probably had not been guilty of Adultery or Fornication. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> saith, there dyed 23000. If there did dye 24000, there must needs dye 23000.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Neither let us tempt <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To tempt in the general notion of the term, signifies to <ns0:hi>make a tryal,</ns0:hi> applied unto God; it signifieth to make a tryal of God, either with reference to his power, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 7.8, 9, 10. or to his truth and goodness; not to be satisfied with Gods word, but to challenge him to a sensible demonstration, is to tempt God: Or else <ns0:hi>tempting</ns0:hi> may signifie more generally, to <ns0:hi>provoke God</ns0:hi>; for indeed all notorious sinning against God is a <ns0:hi>tempting of God,</ns0:hi> not believing the wrath of God, which he hath revealed in his Word against sin, till men feel it.</ns0:note> Christ <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The term <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> here is very remarkable to prove Christs Divine Nature and Existence before he was incarnate; for the same person who is here cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>Christ,</ns0:hi> is called God, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 106.14. and <ns0:hi>Iehovah</ns0:hi> also in the same <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi>; neither could they have tempted Christ at that time, if at that time he had not been existent.</ns0:note>, as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 27.2,</ns0:note> some of them also tempted, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                     </ns0:gap>.9.</ns0:note> were destroyed of ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pents <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Serpents</ns0:hi> he meaneth the fiery Serpents, we have the History, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 21.6, 7</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Murmuring</ns0:hi> signifies the speaking against a <ns0:hi>person</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>thing,</ns0:hi> out of dislike, impatience, or discontent. It was a sin the Jews were very much guilty of, as may be read <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 16.7, 8. <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 14.27. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16.11. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 15.24. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 17.3. <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 16.41. The Apostle may either refer to all their murmurings, when he saith,</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 14.37.</ns0:note> were destroyed of the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroyer <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">they were (as the punishment of their sin) <ns0:hi>destroyed of the destroyer,</ns0:hi> or to that more universal murmuring upon the ill report the Spies brought up of the Land of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> of which we read <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 14.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Now all these things happened to them for <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Types.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> ensamples <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">All these dispensations of Divine Providence in the revela<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions of Divine wrath against several sorts of sinners, happened to the Jews, which were Gods first and ancient people, and enjoyed those great priviledges, which were before mentioned, not only as just punishments upon them for their sins, but as <ns0:hi>Examples</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Types,</ns0:hi> to let the succeeding World know what they should find God towards such kind of sinners,</ns0:note>: and they <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.4. Chap. 9.10.</ns0:note> are written for our ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monition <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">and God in his wise Providence hath ordered the Record of them in holy Writ, that others who should live afterward, might read, and hear, and fear, and take warning, and beware of such wicked actions, as pulled down such vengeance upon a people, than which none can plead to a nearer relation to God, or the recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving of greater favours and priviledges from him.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 4.5. Heb. 10.25.</ns0:note> upon whom the ends of the world are come <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles ordinarily in their Epistles speak of the World, as nigh to an end in their Age, though it hath since continued more than 1600 years; which would incline one to think, that they thought it would have been at an end before this time, but had no such Revelation from God. So true is that of our Saviour, That <ns0:hi>of that day and hour knoweth no man,</ns0:hi> and it should teach us to beware of too particular determinations in the case, which the Apostles did not make, though they spake of theirs as the last times, and themselves as such upon whom the ends of the World were come.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Wherefore <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 11.20.</ns0:note> let him that thinketh that he standeth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Either in a right and sound judgment and opinion of things, or in a state of favour with God, or confirmed in an holy course of life and conversation. <ns0:hi>Standeth in Grace,</ns0:hi> Rom. 5.2. A man may stand in these things, and he may but think that he standeth: be it as it will, he is concerned</ns0:note>, take heed lest he fall <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">to <ns0:hi>take heed lest he fall,</ns0:hi> he may but think he standeth, and if so, he will fall; he may really stand in a right judgment and opinion of things, and be a Member of the Church of Christ, and yet may fall into errours and some loose practices, so as to bring down Divine vengeance upon himself; he may have Gods favour so far as concerns external privilegdes, and yet perish, as many of the Jews did in the instances before mentioned; nay, he may really stand in a state of Justification and Regeneration, and yet may fall, though not <ns0:hi>totally</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>finally,</ns0:hi> yet foully, so as to lose his peace, and bring Gods severe judgments upon him; therefore he that thinketh that he standeth, whether his appre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hensions be false or true, had need use all means and caution that he may not fall, and that because, if he keepeth his stand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, it must be by the use of due means, which God hath ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointed in order to that end, though he be also kept <ns0:hi>by the power of God unto salvation,</ns0:hi> 1 Pet. 1.5.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 There hath no temptation <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Temptation (as hath been said before) signifieth in the general notion of it no more than <ns0:hi>Tryals,</ns0:hi> and is often so used in holy Writ. Now in regard we are tryed either by <ns0:hi>afflictive Providences,</ns0:hi> or by motions made to us, either from God, or our own lusts, or the Devil, or men of the World. <ns0:hi>Temptati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons</ns0:hi> in Scripture sometimes signifie <ns0:hi>Afflictions,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.2. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.6. Sometimes <ns0:hi>motions made to us by God,</ns0:hi> Gen. 22.2. both which sorts of <ns0:hi>Temptations</ns0:hi> are good in themselves. Some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times the term signifies <ns0:hi>Motions</ns0:hi> made by the lusts and unrenew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed part of our own Souls, or by the Devil, or by sinful men in the World; these are <ns0:hi>sinful Temptations,</ns0:hi> and what we most or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinarily call by that name. Whether the Apostle here means all or some of these, cannot certainly be determined; what he saith is true of all, and therefore that is the safest interpretation of the term in this place, though he had not been before speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing indeed of afflictive Temptations. He had before affright<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed them with minding them of the possibility of their falling, though they did stand, or thought they stood, and cautioned them to take heed: Here he comforteth them, by minding them,</ns0:note> taken you, but what is <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>moderate.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> common to man <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">that no temptation had befallen them, but what was incident and common to men, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and they could not expect to be freed from the common Fate of Mankind:</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 1.9.</ns0:note> God is faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 125.3. 2 Pet. 2.9.</ns0:note> who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">then he minds them, that that God who had promised strength and assistance to his people, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 7.11. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 11.13. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.18. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.4. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 3.3. was one that would be as good as his word, being <ns0:hi>faithful,</ns0:hi> and would not suffer them to be tempted above their strength, and ability to oppose and resist;</ns0:note>; but will with the temptation also <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 29.11.</ns0:note> make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">yea, and would make a way to escape, both the evil of the temptation, that it should not over-bear them to a total ruine of their Souls, and likewise the burdensom and affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctive evil, that it should not continually lie upon them, provi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded they used their just endeavours, and (as he had said be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore) <ns0:hi>took heed</ns0:hi> lest they fell.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:448" />14 Wherefore, my dearly beloved, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 6.17. 1 Joh. 5.21.</ns0:note> flee from idolatry <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Apostle would have them avoid all sin, but Idolatry more especially, keeping at the utmost distance imaginable from that, being of all sins in its kind the greatest transgression; up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on which account it is often in Scripture compared to Whore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, though we ought to be afraid of, and to decline all sin; yet as God hath revealed his wrath against any particular sin more than other, so every good Christian is obliged more to detest and abhor that sin. How the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> were concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in this caution, we shall read afterwards <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. For though <ns0:hi>Idolatry</ns0:hi> be properly where the failure is in the ultimate or me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diate object of our Worship, and the Creature is made either the ultimate term of our Worship, or the <ns0:hi>medium</ns0:hi> in and <ns0:hi>by which</ns0:hi> we worship the Creator; yet there are many other ways by which we may be partakers of the sins of others, and this sin of Idolatry in particular: and <ns0:hi>Idolatry</ns0:hi> being a sin of the greatest magnitude, from which they were bound to keep the furthest distance, they were bound to take heed of being parta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kers of other mens sins of this kind.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">I speak as to wise men: judge ye what I say <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">As to the present case, you are persons that understand the Principles of Christian Religion, I will make you Judges in this case.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matt. 26.26.</ns0:note> The cup of blessing which we bless <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">It is on all hands agreed, That the Apostle is here speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of Believers communicating in the Sacrament of the Lords Supper; by the <ns0:hi>Cup of blessing,</ns0:hi> he meaneth the Cup there, which he so calleth, because we in the taking of it bless the Lord, who gave his Son to die for us; and Christ for that great love which he shewed in dying for us, we are said to bless it, because we by solemn Prayer in the Consecration of it, set it apart for that sacred use, and beg of God to bless it to us.</ns0:note>, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This <ns0:hi>Cup</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) is <ns0:hi>the Communion of the blood of Christ.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Cup</ns0:hi> is put for the Wine in the Cup (which is very ordinary) the <ns0:hi>Cup</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Wine</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Blessing</ns0:hi> signifieth that Cup of Wine to which the bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing is added, or with which in that holy Institution we thank<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully remember the Death of Christ, and bless his Name for that great mercy, and the <ns0:hi>Wine</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Cup of blessing,</ns0:hi> also here signifieth our religious Action in drinking of that Cup of Wine so blessed, This, saith he, is <ns0:hi>the Communion of the blood of Christ,</ns0:hi> that is, it is an Action whereby and wherein Christ communicates himself and his Grace to us, and we communicate our Souls to him; so that Christ and Believers in that Action have a mutual Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />munion one with another:</ns0:note>? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">And as it is with the one Ele<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment in that holy Sacrament, so it is also with the other. The Bread which the Minister breaketh (according to the Institution and Example of Christ) for the Church to make use of in the Celebration of the Lords Supper, that is, their Action in eating of that Bread so broken, and divided amongst them<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> is the Communion of the Body of Christ<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> an Action wherein Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians have a Fellowship and Communion with Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 12.5. Chap. 12.27.</ns0:note> we being many, are one bread and one body <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Believers, though many, yet are one Body, and declare themselves to be one Body mystical, by their fellowshi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther in the Ordinance of the Lords Supper; as the Bread they there eat is one Bread, though it be made up of many grains of Corn, which come into the composition of that Loaf or piece of Bread which is so broken, distributed, and eaten; and the Wine they drink is one Cup, one Body of Wine, though it be made up of many particular Grapes.</ns0:note>: for we are all partakers of that one bread <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">And they declare themselves to be one Body, by their joynt partaking of that one Bread. Some have from hence fetched an Argument to prove the unlawfulness of communicating with scandalous sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners at the Lords Table, because we declare our selves one Bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy with those that communicate: but whether it will (if exa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mined) be cogent enough, I doubt; for <ns0:hi>one Body</ns0:hi> signifieth no more than one Church, and that not invisible, but visible. So as we only declare our selves to be fellow-members of the visi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Church with those with whom we partake in that Ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nance, and the visible Church may consist of persons that are <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ad mixed with the good. So as, though undoubtedly scan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dalously wicked persons ought to be excluded from the holy Table, yea, and no Unbeliever hath a right to it: yet it may reasonably be doubted, whether those that partake with Unbe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lievers, do by it owne themselves to be Unbelievers, they only owne themselves Members of that Church, wherein there are some Unbelievers. But the scope of the Apostle is from hence to argue, That by a parity of reason, those that communicated with an idolatrous Assembly in their Sacrifices, declared them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves by that action to be one Body with those Idolaters.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Behold Israel after the flesh <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> after the flesh, was the whole seed of <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> the whole Body of the Jewish Church; for Believers only were <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> after the Spirit, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.6. called the <ns0:hi>Israel of God, Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.16.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 3.3.7.15.</ns0:note> are not they which eat of the sacrifices, partakers of the altar? <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">If in the Jewish Church any persons ate of the flesh of Sacrifices offered upon Gods Altar, did they not by that act manifest, that they were Members of the Jewish Church, and owned that God, to whom those Sacrifices were offered, and that way of Worship by which God was so worshipped. By the same reason these <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> eating of the flesh of those Beasts in the Idols Temple, which had been offered unto Idols, did by that act declare their owning of the Idol, and that ido<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />latrous Worship which had been there performed, and were really partakers of the idolatrous Altar.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 What say I then? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 8.4.</ns0:note> that the idol is any thing, or that which is sacrificed to idols is any thing? <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">I do not by this contradict what I before said, nor now affirm, that an Idol is any thing, or the Sacrifices offered to it any thing. An Idol hath nothing in it of a Dei<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>y, nor can it either sanctifie, or pollute any thing that is set before it; the errour is in your action, as you communicate with such as are Idolaters; it is your own action that polluteth you, not the Idol, nor yet the meat set before it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 But <ns0:hi>I say,</ns0:hi> that the things which the Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 17.7<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Deut. 32.17<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Psal. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>6. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Rev. 9.20.</ns0:note> sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The Heathens might not intentionally offer Sacrifices to Devils (such a thing can hardly be supposed of men) but actual<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, they offered their Sacrifices to Devils; for they were De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vils, that is, evil Angels, which deluded the poor Heathen, and gave Answers from the Images and Statues which they wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shipped, believing the true God to be in them: which Answers they accounted for Oracles. Besides, the Apostle saith, they sacrificed to Devils, because in Gods esteem it was so, though not in their intention; God judgeth of mens acts of Worship and Homage pretendedly done unto him, not according to their intention, but according to the truth and reality of the thing: Now really the Heathen in their Sacrifices paid an Ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mage to Devils, though such a thing was far from their inten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and this deserves the consideration, both of the <ns0:hi>Papists,</ns0:hi> who worship Images, and also of those <ns0:hi>Protestants</ns0:hi> (if any such be) who would excuse the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> in their Idolatries from their <ns0:hi>intentions.</ns0:hi> The Nature of Idolatry doth not lye in mens intending to worship the Creature instead of the Creator (there were hardly ever any such Idolaters in the World) but in their actual doing of the thing; and except they can find a direct Rule in holy Writ ordering the Adoration of the Creator in the Creature, or before the Creature, it is much to be fe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ed, that in the last day God will judge their Homage performed to the Creature, not to him.</ns0:note>: and I would not that ye should have fel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowship with devils <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Now, saith the Apostle, you had need take heed that by this action, you prove not your selves to have fellowship with Devils instead of Christ and the true and living God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Cor. 8.</ns0:note> Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">We may either take the phrase as signifying all religio<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s Communion under one great Act of Religion, or as particularly signifying, having a Communion with Christ in the Ordinance of the Lords Supper, which is called the <ns0:hi>Cup of the Lord,</ns0:hi> either because God hath instituted and appointed the drinking of it, or because it is done for the honour, glory, and remembrance of our Lord Christ, to <ns0:hi>remember his death until he come</ns0:hi> (as the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle speaketh <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 11.) This the Apostle tells them they could not <ns0:hi>drink</ns0:hi> of, that is, not rightly, and with a good conscience; or not <ns0:hi>really,</ns0:hi> no man that is an Idolater, or hath Communion with Idolaters in their idolatrous Acts, can have Communion with Christ:</ns0:note>, and the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 32.</ns0:note> cup of devils <ns0:hi>s</ns0:hi>: ye cannot be partakers of the Lords table, and of the table of devils <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>me is meant by <ns0:hi>the Table of the Lord,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the Table of Devils.</ns0:hi> So as I cannot see how either an <ns0:hi>idolatrous Church</ns0:hi> can be a <ns0:hi>true Church,</ns0:hi> or an Idolater a true Christian, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less we will assert, That a Body of people may be a true Church, that can have no Communion with Christ; or a man may be a true Christian, and yet have no Communion with Christ. Ido<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />latry doubtless both divides the Soul from Christ, as he is the Head of a Believer, and as he is the Head of the Church. To call any Body of Idolaters a true Church, either <ns0:hi>Morally,</ns0:hi> or Metaphysically, is to say to those <ns0:hi>Ammi, You are the Lords peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple,</ns0:hi> to whom God hath said <ns0:hi>Loammi.</ns0:hi> Let them be what they will, the name of a Church belongeth not to them, if (as the Apostle affirmeth) they can have no Communion with Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:448" />22 Do we <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 32.21.</ns0:note> provoke the Lord to jealousie <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Jealousie is a violent passion in a man, not bearing a Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />panion or a Rival as to a thing or person which he loveth. It is in holy Writ applied unto God, not to signifie any such extra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vagancy, excess, or vehemence, as attendeth that passion in men, but only his just displeasure at the giving that Homage to any Creature, which is due to him alone. It is most applied to God to express his anger against those who give Divine Homage to Idols. The Worship of God being a great piece of his glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry which he hath said <ns0:hi>he will not give to another, nor his praise to graven images,</ns0:hi> Isa. 42.8. Hence Divines observe, That jea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lousie is attributed to God in the second Commandment, which concerns the more external Worship of God, to deter men from the violation of it, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20.5. So <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 34.14. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4.20. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 5.9. & 6.15. and in many other Texts, it signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fieth, that the <ns0:hi>Worship of God</ns0:hi> is a thing that he is very tender of, and that his will is to endure no Creature to share with him in it, and that his wrath shall flame against that man, that offers to make any Creature such a sharer.</ns0:note>? Are we stronger then he? <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">So that it is not safe for any to do any thing of that nature, unless he could fansie himself to be stronger than God; for he that doth it, must expect the power and strength of God to be ingaged against him. Thus the Apostle hath disswaded them from eating meat sacrificed to Idols in the Idols Temple, from the <ns0:hi>impiety</ns0:hi> of it, it being a <ns0:hi>Species</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Idolatry,</ns0:hi> against which God hath signally revealed his wrath. He returns in the following verses to an Argument, by which he had before disswaded it, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 8. as it was against <ns0:hi>Charity,</ns0:hi> and the duty of <ns0:hi>Love,</ns0:hi> in which they were indebted to their Brethren.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.12.</ns0:note> All things are lawful for me <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>All things</ns0:hi> here must necessarily signifie <ns0:hi>many things,</ns0:hi> or at least (as some think) all those things I have spoken of, to <ns0:hi>eat <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> offered to Idols,</ns0:hi> &c. But if we interpret it in the latter sense, it is not true without limitations; for the Apostle had but now determined, that to eat meat offered to Idols in the Idols Temple, was to have Communion with Devils. I had rather therefore interpret <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>many,</ns0:hi> as that universal Particle must be interpreted in a great multitude of Scriptures. So as the sense is, There are <ns0:hi>many things</ns0:hi> that are lawful which are not <ns0:hi>expedient,</ns0:hi> that is, considered in themselves under due cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances, they are lawful, but considered in such and such circumstances, are not so, because they are not for the profit, or good, but the hurt and disadvantage of others. Thus the Apostle himself expounds it in the latter clause of the verse, where he saith, they <ns0:hi>edifie not,</ns0:hi> that is, they tend not to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mote the Gospel, or the <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Holiness</ns0:hi> of particular Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians.</ns0:note>, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edifie not <ns0:hi>y.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.1, 2. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2.4.</ns0:note> Let no man seek his own, but anothers wealth <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">It is the duty of every one who is a Disciple of Christ, not meerly to look at his own pleasure, or profit, but the profit and advantage of others, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 13.5. <ns0:hi>Charity seeketh not her own</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) that is, it seeketh not its own with the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>udice of another. So as admit, that in this practice there were nothing looked like Idolatry and impiety towards God, yet <ns0:hi>Charity</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> to your Brethren ought to deter you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">It is possible that Butchers, before they brought their meat into the market, might offer some part of it to the Idol; or it is possible that the <ns0:hi>Priests,</ns0:hi> who had a share in the beasts offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to Idols; or the people that had offered such beasts, who also had a share returned them, might out of covetousness come and bring it to be sold in the market. The Apostle di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />re<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eth the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> in such cases to make no scruple, but eat of it, if it were commonly sold in the shambles, which argued, that the thing in it self, considered nakedly, was not sinful;</ns0:note>, asking no question for conscience sake <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">but yet he would have them in that case ask no questions whence it came? Or whether it had not been offered to an Idol? for the sake of other mens consciences, lest some others standing by, should take notice, that they bought and ate such me<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t. Or their own <ns0:hi>Consciences,</ns0:hi> lest though the thing in it self, so separated from a sacred use, and returned to its com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon use, might be lawfully eaten, yet their consciences should afterwards reflect upon them for the doing of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 19.5. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 10.14. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>0.12.</ns0:note> For the earth is the Lords, and the fulness thereof <ns0:note n="c" place="margin">This sentence is taken out of <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 24.1. The Earth is Gods, or the Lord Christs, who hath sanctified all things for the use of man, and all the variety of creatures that are in it are sanctified by him. An Idol cannot pollute any kind of meat, it hath no such malign influence upon any thing, you may pol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lute your selves by your action, eating it in the Idols Temple, at an Idolaters Feast immediately upon his Sacrifice, but the Idol it self is no operative thing, nor can cause an ill quality in the meat; let the meat be once returned to its common use (the Idolaters sacred Mysteries being over) it is the Lords, what he hath appointed for the use of man. In the Idols Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple they took the meat out of the Devils hand, that was indeed unlawful: but if it were once returned to its common use, and sold in the market, they took it out of the hand of Gods com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon Providence, and the <ns0:hi>Creatures of God are good, and not to be refused, if they be received with thanksgiving,</ns0:hi> 1 Tim. 4.4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 If any of them which believe not, bid you to <ns0:hi>a feast</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Apostle puts another case, in which they might law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully enough eat of meat offered to an Idol, that was in case any of their Neighbours that were Heathens, invited them to dinner or supper in a private house (some add, or in the Idols Temple, if it were a Feast of friendship, not a Feast upon a Sacrifice, but I doubt that; and also whether in the Idol-Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples there were any Feasts but upon Sacrifices)</ns0:note>, and ye be disposed to go, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 10.7.</ns0:note> whatsoever is set before you eat <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">he determi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neth it lawful for them to go and eat whatsoever was set before them; but in this case he would also have them <ns0:hi>ask no questions for conscience sake.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, asking no questions for conscience sake.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 But if any man say unto you, This is offered in sacrifice unto idols, eat not <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The meat being out of the Idols Temple, and returned to a common use, there could be no impiety in eating it, no com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />munion with Devils, and partaking of the Table of Devils, in and by such an action; but yet there might be a breach of Charity in the action, that is, in case one were there pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent, who knew that it had been so offered to the Idol, and declared his offence, by telling the Christian that was about to eat, that that meat had been so offered, in that case the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle commandeth Christians</ns0:note> for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 8.10, 11.</ns0:note> his sake that shewed it, and for conscience sake <ns0:note n="⸪" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>not to eat,</ns0:hi> and that partly <ns0:hi>for his sake</ns0:hi> that shewed it, lest they should lay a stumbling-block before him, and by their example imbolden him that shewed it to do the like, though he doubted the lawfulness of it; and likewise for conscience sake, that is, for their own conscience sake, which through weakness might afterward trouble them for it, though without just cause.</ns0:note>: For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 10.14, Psal. 24.1. Vers. 26.</ns0:note> the earth is the Lords, and the fulness thereof <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He gives them as a reason for it, <ns0:hi>Because the earth is the Lords, and the fulness thereof,</ns0:hi> that is, because there was other meat enough to eat. This passage taken out of the <ns0:hi>Psalmist</ns0:hi> had a something different application, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 26. there the Apostle used it to justifie the <ns0:hi>lawfulness</ns0:hi> of their eating such meat, returned again to a common use, and exposed to sale in the shambles: here he useth it to disswade them from eating, if any let them know it had been offered to the Idol.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the others <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">By reason of what we had, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 28. (where the Apostle for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bad eating these meats, in case any of the Feast told them they had been offered to Idols, both <ns0:hi>for his sake that told him so</ns0:hi>; and <ns0:hi>also for conscience sake</ns0:hi>) it is most reasonable to interpret those words, <ns0:hi>not thine own</ns0:hi> in this verse, <ns0:hi>not thine own only,</ns0:hi> there being frequent instances in Scripture, where the Negative Particle must be so restrained, as <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.42. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.27, 38.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 14.16.</ns0:note> why is my liberty judged by ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther mans conscience? <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">For why should my practice in a thing, wherein I have a li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />berty, be censured or condemned by the conscience of another, he being perswaded, that what I do and judge that I have a liberty to do, and may do lawfully, is done by me sinfully, and I by him accounted a transgressor for it; so as, though I do a thing that is <ns0:hi>honest,</ns0:hi> yet it is not honest in the sight of all men, or of good report, whereas Christians are obliged, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.17. to <ns0:hi>provide things honest in the sight of all men,</ns0:hi> not in his own sight meerly, and to do those things that are <ns0:hi>lovely</ns0:hi> and of <ns0:hi>good report</ns0:hi> Phil. 3.8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 For if I by <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>thanksgi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> grace be a partaker <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">If I by the <ns0:hi>goodness of God,</ns0:hi> whose the Earth is, and the fulness thereof; or by the <ns0:hi>Grace of Knowledge,</ns0:hi> by which God hath given me to understand that I may do that, as to which others less knowing stumble, can eat such meat (out of the Idols Temple) as part of it hath been offered to the Idol; or <ns0:hi>with Thanksgiving</ns0:hi> partake of such<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> meat (for so <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> signifies <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 6.32. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 17.9.)</ns0:note>, why am I evil spoken of, for that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Tim. 4.3, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>,</ns0:note> for which I give thanks? <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Why am I <ns0:hi>blasphemed,</ns0:hi> or evilly spo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken of, for that which I can give God thanks? That is, I ought not to cause another to speak evil of me for using of meat, but rather than run that danger, to abstain from such meat which I could otherwise eat of, and give God thanks: For in so doing I should but abuse my liberty, and instead of giving God thanks, I should grievously offend God, not at all consulting his Glory.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col 3.17.</ns0:note> Whether therefore ye eat or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The Apostle in these three last verses, layeth down three Rules, to direct Christians how to use their liberty as to things that are of an indifferent nature, neither in themselves com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded nor forbidden in the Word of God. His first Rule is in this verse, <ns0:hi>To do whatsoever we do to the glory of God.</ns0:hi> This is a general Rule, not to be restrained to the eating of meat of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fered to Idols, of which the former discourse had been. It is a general Rule, not applicable alone to eating and drinking, but to all other humane actions. The reasonableness of this Rule appeareth from our consideration, That the Glory of God was the End of our Creation, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 16.4. <ns0:hi>The Lord hath made all things for himself:</ns0:hi> and indeed it is impossible it should be otherwise; for whereas every reasonable Agent both propounds to himself some end of his actions, and the best end he can imagine, it is impossible but that God also in creating man, should propound to himself some End, and there being no bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter end than his own Glory, he could propound no other unto himself. The Glory of God being the end which he pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pounded to himself in creating man, it must needs follow, that that must be the chief and greatest end which any man can pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pound to himself in his actions. God is then glorified by us, when by our means, or by occasion of us, he is well spoken of in the World, or by our obedience to his Will: This our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour hath taught us, <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 17.4, 6. No man in any of his actions hath a liberty from this Rule, so as, though a man, as to many things, hath a liberty to marry, or not to marry, to eat meats, or not to eat them, to wear this apparel, or not to wear it; yet he is not even in such things as these so at liberty, but he ought to look about, and to consider circumstances, which will be most for the honour of God, the credit of the Gospel, and reputation of Religion. And the judgment of this is to be made from circumstances, the difference of which may make that unlawful, which otherwise would be lawful, and that lawful, which under other circumstances would be unlaw<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:449" />32 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 14.13. 2 Cor. 6.3.</ns0:note> Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>Greeks.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Gentiles <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">We use to say, that men are offended when they are grieved or anger'd; but these offences are not here meant (as appears by the <ns0:hi>Greek Phrase,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>) but give no occasion of sin or stumbling. This care he commands us, with refe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence to all men; for at that time all the World fell under one of these denominations, they were either <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> (that is, Heathens) or the <ns0:hi>Church of God</ns0:hi> (that is, Christians) it was always an hard matter, if not a thing impossible, for Christians to carry themselves so, as not to anger those that were no Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians; but it was not impossible for them so to behave them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, as not to be to them any just occasion of sin:</ns0:note> nor to the church of God <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Much less ought conscientious Christians to give offence to Christians, that made up the Church of God, and were with them Mem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bers of the same mystical Body, of which Christ is the Head.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 Even as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.2. Chap. 9.19, 22.</ns0:note> I please all men in all things <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That is, in all things wherein the Law of God hath left me a liberty; for <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> pleased no man, either in the omission of any thing which God had commanded him to do, or in the doing of any thing which God had forbidden him to do,</ns0:note>, not seeking mine own profit, but the <ns0:hi>profit</ns0:hi> of ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny, that they might be saved <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">not seeking my own advantage, either the satisfaction of my own mind, or humor, or my own gain, but the advantage of others, especially in matters that may any way affect them as to their eternal Salvation. Thus <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> like a good Shepherd, goeth out before the sheep, and leadeth them, and as every true Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nister should be himself an example to the flock of Christ. And this is a third Rule to be observed by Christians, as to the use of the liberty which Gods Law hath lest them as to any par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular actions, notwithstanding that liberty, yet they ought to have respect to the spiritual good and Salvation of others, and to do that part which their judgments inform them, will be, as least, to the spiritual damage and detriment, so most to the spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual good and profit of the Souls of others with whom they converse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
